extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in humor theory (psychology, linguistics, philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of major theoretical frameworks that explain what humor is, what makes something humorous, and the functions of humor across psychology, linguistics, philosophy, and evolution. Useful for studying, comparing, or applying humor theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relief theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggests humor is a mechanism for pent-up emotions or tension through emotional relief; laughter serves as a homeostatic mechanism by which psychological stress is reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor relieves tension (e.g., tickling), releases 'psychic energy' mobilized by false expectations (Herbert Spencer, Freud), and is used to overcome sociocultural inhibitions and reveal suppressed desires. Researchers cite examples, studies (Shurcliff; Zillmann & Bryant), and applications to drama (Samuel Johnson, Dryden). Distinguishes tendentious (victim-based) vs non-tendentious humor; innocuous cues can make hostile elements socially acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims people laugh at the misfortunes of others because they feel superior; laughter is the sudden glory one feels that one is better than the target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated with Hobbes, Plato, Aristotle. Hobbes lists typical triggers (unexpected success, perception of defects in others/past, abstracted absurdity). Includes nuance: Aristotle ties incongruity and hostility; Kant allows harmless teasing. Discussion includes how the theory is sometimes read prescriptively (use of targets in comedy). Critics argue many types of humor don't involve superiority and that feelings of superiority are distinct from humor itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective disposition theory
rubrics_metrics.description: In media and entertainment, audiences make moral judgments and attitudes (dispositions) toward characters affect humorous experience; amusement depends on whether good things happen to good people or bad things to bad people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies directional rules: stronger negative disposition toward the disparaged agent increases mirth; stronger positive disposition toward the disparaged agent decreases mirth; for victors, negative disposition decreases mirth and positive increases it. Explains role of liking for performer and links to 'punching up' vs 'punching down' ethical framing. Notes that severe tragedy can overpower mirth (pity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggests humor and laughter rely on incongruity — anything contrary to expectation according to some norm — often resolved by a punchline or shift in perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers linguistic examples (puns, riddles), cognitive dissonance and resolution (incongruity-resolution), and philosophers (Hutcheson, Kant, Schopenhauer, Bergson). Emphasizes surprise, cognitive shift, and resolution; includes variants emphasizing simultaneity of contrast vs mental shift. Incongruity may combine with relief or superiority mechanisms and occurs across verbal and nonverbal humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign Violation Theory (BVT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor occurs when: (1) something threatens one's sense of how the world ought to be, (2) the threatening situation seems benign, and (3) a person sees both interpretations at the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains tickling/play fighting and extensions to dignity, linguistic, social, and moral norm violations. Benignity can arise from competing norms, psychological distance, or weak commitment to a norm. Predicts individual/context differences (e.g., churchgoers less amused by church-violation examples). Useful for explaining why jokes can be funny to some and offensive to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script-based Semantic Theory of Humor (SSTH)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal-humor-focused theory: to produce humor the text must be compatible with two different semantic scripts and those scripts must be opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke's punchline triggers an abrupt switch from the primary script to the secondary opposing script. Scripts are large semantic frames evoked by words; examples include DOCTOR vs LOVER. Provides a finite, culturally dependent list of script oppositions (actual/non-actual, normal/abnormal, possible/impossible, good/bad, life/death, obscene/non-obscene, etc.). Emphasizes that scripts must be cleverly tied to make 'pseudo-sense' rather than mere juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Theory of Verbal Humor (GTVH)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension of SSTH which models verbal jokes across six independent Knowledge Resources (KRs) to analyze and compare jokes' similarity and generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GTVH orders KRs hierarchically (higher KRs constrain lower ones) and expands SSTH to cover longer humorous texts beyond simple jokes. It is used to represent, compare, and generate joke variants (e.g., light bulb jokes) by manipulating KRs. Empirical testing of KR ordering has been attempted with partial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Script opposition (SO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Script opposition references the script opposition included in Raskin's SSTH (themes such as real/unreal, actual/non-actual, normal/abnormal, possible/impossible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SO is the top-level KR that constrains choices in lower resources; selecting an SO (e.g., DUMB/SMART) reduces options for targets and other parameters. Central to how jokes set up competing interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Logical mechanism (LM)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanism which connects the different scripts in the joke; ranges from simple verbal techniques (pun) to complex faulty logic or false analogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LM explains how the switch between scripts is achieved (pun, ambiguity resolution, analogy, faulty inference). It is a core determiner of the joke's cognitive operation and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Situation (SI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes the objects, activities, instruments, and props needed to tell the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SI defines contextual elements and settings required for a joke's instantiation; altering SI can create new variants while keeping other KRs constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Target (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies the actor(s) who become the 'butt' of the joke, developing stereotypes of groups, professions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TA is optional but central to many jokes; choices here interact with cultural stereotypes and ethical considerations (punching up/down). TA can be constrained by SO and influence audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Narrative strategy (NS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses the narrative format of the joke (simple narrative, dialogue, riddle) and classifies genres and subgenres of verbal humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NS allows GTVH to represent all comedic texts (not just short jokes), including oral and printed narratives of any length. NS choices affect pacing, timing, and presentation of incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: GTVH — Language (LA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contains information necessary for the verbalization of the text: exact wording and placement of functional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LA is responsible for the surface realization of a joke (word-choice, syntax, prosody). Small changes in LA can affect ambiguity, timing, and thus funniness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer model of humor (Suslov)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposes a general information-processing malfunction (deletion of a false version) plus timing as an algorithmic basis for humor; links to incongruity-resolution and neural-network realizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes deletion of false versions from consciousness corresponding to zeroing neural network parts and excess neuronal energy producing motor responses (laughter). Applies to verbal, visual, and tickling humor; explains individual susceptibility, role of timing, intonation, and absence of effect from trite jokes. Suggests biological origin with later social functions and calls for extensive databases for practical realization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribution theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes an audience's inability to precisely identify what is funny and why; people misattribute laughter to innocuous elements while underlying tendentious/hostile elements drive the reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Freud and formalized by Zillmann & Bryant (1980). Tendentious elements (taboo, hostility) create laughter while audiences believe they laugh at innocent jokework. Explains transferred excitation and how hostility can be disguised by innocuous features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontic-epistemic theory of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Posits laughter is a reaction to a cognitive impasse where social being appears no longer real (a momentary epistemological difficulty), causing perception of factual reality to trump social reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marteinson's theory describes mechanisms like Deculturation (factual disproves social reality) and Relativisation (social reality contradicting itself). Laughter resets social perception, anesthetizes the mind with euphoria, permits forgetting the comic stimulus, and communicates the humorous reaction socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection theory of humor (Geoffrey Miller)
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues humor evolved via sexual selection as an indicator of traits like intelligence rather than having direct survival value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions humor as a fitness indicator attractive to mates; used to explain selection pressures for humorous ability in human evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection of mistaken reasoning theory (Hurley, Dennett, Adams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposes humor evolved because it strengthens the brain's ability to find mistakes in active belief structures (detect mistaken reasoning), enhancing problem-solving capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames humor as adaptive for improving practical reasoning and decision-making; somewhat consistent with sexual selection in marking cognitive abilities but emphasizes survival value through better problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as defense mechanism (Vaillant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifies humor as a level-4 defense mechanism: overt expression of ideas and feelings (often unpleasant) that gives pleasure to others; wit as displacement (level-3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor allows addressing distressing subjects by exploring absurdity; distinguishes humor from wit (wit skirts around distressing thoughts). Useful for clinical/psychological interpretation of humor's intrapersonal function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of humor vs sense of seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: One must have both senses to distinguish what is to be taken literally; especially needed when humor is used to make a serious point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological research examines how audiences interpret humorous intent (e.g., court jesters conveying serious info). Also warns about 'bad taste' where humor crosses a line and is taken seriously (offense). Context and audience interpretation are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor, metonymy, and allegory in humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Roles of metaphor, metonymy, conceptual blending, and poetic metaphor in generating humor, especially in linguistic/computational approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tony Veale and others use structure-mapping, conceptual metaphor theory, and blending to formalize humor mechanisms. Bakhtin's 'poetic metaphor' and allegorization also account for literary humor. These mechanisms inform computational and cognitive models of verbal humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: O'Shannon model of the comedic event
rubrics_metrics.description: A unified framework integrating context, information, aspects of awareness, and enhancers/inhibitors to explain comedic reception and response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context (reception factors), information (cognitive processing and degree of incongruity), aspects of awareness (internal reality, external role, effect on context/others), and enhancers/inhibitors (superiority, relief, aggression, identification, shock) interact to determine response. Explains why humor can rely on different mechanisms and how low-incongruity wordplay produces appreciative responses vs visceral reactions from high incongruity; includes timing and evolutionary accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnoticed fall-back to former behavior patterns model
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines laughter as an acoustic signal indicating an unnoticed fall-back to former behaviour patterns; partially unifies superiority and incongruity theories and links to ticklishness and bipedalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Posits laughter functions to make others aware of an unnoticed behavioral reversion, explaining overlaps between superiority and incongruity perspectives and connecting play/tickling to humor evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bergson's theory of the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Argues the fundamental source of the comic is 'mechanism applied to life' — rigidity and mechanical behavior in beings whose essence is movement and elasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter is a social/moral corrective condemning eccentric or rigid behavior; comic situations include fall, imitation, automatic application of rules, absent-mindedness, and repetitive gestures. Bergson treats laughter as an intellectual (detached) activity that enforces uniformity of behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex systems theory applied to humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies complexity/chaos theory to explain how interacting parts of a complex system (language, discourse community) give rise to collective humorous behavior and how humor changes over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for transdisciplinary research; applications include studies of incongruity-resolution dynamics (Tschacher & Haken) and conversational humor lifecycle (Demjén). Useful for modeling emergence, spread, and decline of jokes/memes in discourse communities.
